newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka rules out mediation to end rebel war.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka rules out mediation to end rebel war.

text.p: Sri Lanka on Thursday ruled out third-party mediation to end a 13-year-old separatist war, saying the conflict was an internal matter that had to be resolved by the government and Tamil rebels.
"Third parties coming here is absolutely out of the question. This is an internal matter," Foreign Minister Lakshman Kadirgamar told Reuters in an interview.
He said several governments, individuals and non-governmental organisations in the past had offered out of goodwill to help end the war, but Sri Lanka wanted to talk to the rebels directly.
"It (mediation) becomes an interference in our internal affairs and we will not tolerate it at all," Kadirgamar said.
The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) are battling government troops for an independent homeland in the island's north and east.
The government says more than 50,000 people have died since the conflict began in 1983. The LTTE says the figure is much higher.
An LTTE spokesman told Reuters from London that the rebel group was keen to involve a third party to resolve the conflict.
"LTTE is interested in third-party mediation to solve the conflict in Sri Lanka. It's in the interest of peace in the island that we seek third-party mediation," Anton Rajah said over the telephone.

But Kadirgamar said the LTTE were not serious about mediation. "The LTTE has no serious intention for mediation apart from making noises across the world to buy time to regroup as they have done successfully in the past," he said.
Britain said late last year it was willing to mediate a settlement between the Sri Lankan government and separatist Tamils if invited by Colombo and rebels.

Sri Lankan newspapers reported in December that a representative of International Alert, a conflict resolution group, was in Colombo and was expected to meet the LTTE leaders in the northeast of the island to help revive peace talks.
Kadirgamar said while parties offering to help had a legitimate line of thinking, they did not realise the kind of institution the LTTE was.
"They (LTTE) are unique in this century. Anywhere in time. We believe that LTTE is firmly committed to a separate state and to winning it by force," he said.
Kadirgamar accused the LTTE of unilaterally breaking off peace talks launched by Sri Lanka after President Chandrika Kumaratunga's People's Alliance won power in 1994 general elections.

"Our position is very simple. The LTTE is an aggressor because in April 1995 they broke off the talks unilaterally. They did not give it a chance to blossom and to grow. They took the view that force is the only way to get their separate state," he said.
The last round of peace talks broke down after the LTTE attacked a naval boat in the eastern port of Trincomalee in April 1995, sparking renewed fighting.
